criticals.note: Claim is right at the player-contract level: no doc states what Epoch 1 asks of the player moment to moment, the verb set on a thread (the Writing Desk, Office pretexts, Quiet Claims, illicit funds, letters are listed but not tied to a thread loop), what failure looks like beyond persecution/extraction (extracted_overt is the only defined loss state, DESIGN_NOTES.md:147), or what the epoch-end evaluation displays. 'Leverage Chain' is named in 3 places and never defined; true. But 'no document' overstates: a macro goal (climb the ladder under a tech ceiling), a two-ledger epoch-end design, a failure path and an end-of-epoch gate exist. The design deliberately rejects a single score. Strongest counter: a solo owner of a young project can discover the loop by building, and the roadmap marks every future change 'planned - revisable'. That defence is weak for this particular gap because the document set is already unusually specified (27 changes, hundreds of numeric parameters) so the loop is being constrained by specs written before it exists. It does not win fully: the gap is a risk, not a defect. Major, not critical.

criticals.note: The 'HUD explicitly banned' premise is wrong: line 207 constrains only travel-cabin surface cues and says so. The notes plainly rely on advisor briefings, Writing Desk replies, the Wider World Overview and the Drone's tells as feedback channels, and the architecture-level choice 'diegetic parchment and neural lace remain the later player-facing surface' (DESIGN_NOTES.md:218) is the intended answer. What survives: no passage specifies how a covert action's success/notice/backfire is reported per action (when, how legible, how delayed), and the discovery layers and pressure stocks are only exposed through predicates on cues and advisor tells. That is an under-specified mapping, not a missing system. Counter-argument (owner will tune feedback through play) is reasonable since legibility is empirically tuned. Major at most; the wording 'banned' must be corrected.

criticals.note: The sequencing observation holds: the first real content pack lands at 11, first consequential choice at 07b, and no human-read test of writing or fun is scheduled before then; 07e does test voice by fixture. 'Built against an empty world' is overstated: a proving slice with a walkable player and an NPC exists and 05c-05e make it playable. Also 05a/05b/09/10 are big systems queued before content. Counter-argument: the sequence is explicitly revisable, the owner is front-loading engine contracts because the design is multi-epoch and plug-and-play, and a determinism-first sim legitimately needs infrastructure before content. That defence is partly valid but ignores the claim's real point: nothing forces a fun check. Major process risk, not critical.

routes.fit: Compatible with every pillar. The slice uses seed exemplars (Sorrel/Pell, Highglass Hold) that DESIGN_NOTES.md:36 calls non-exhaustive writing-quality bars, and the proving-slice, 05c shell, 05d locomotion and 05e menus are already archived or specified to host it. Does not conflict with epoch-agnostic rules as long as the thread is authored through the registries.
routes.cost: Moderate: re-order roadmap so 07 (paging), 07b (pretext choice) and a minimal thread/ledger diff come ahead of 05a/05b/06; author one tiny pack; end card via existing renderer. Little throwaway work if kept registry-based.
routes.risk: Slice grows into a mini-11 or hardcodes feudal content in domain/application (AGENTS.md ban). Also a thin slice may not exercise Regard or Inertia and so understates systems value.
routes.note: Highest-value route and a direct answer to S1-03. Keep it inside the registries, make it the acceptance gate for 06.
